name: Erik Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. This is confidential, so tell me both what you would say publicly and what you think alone. What does your normal day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Erik, 43, a mid-level developer at a tech company that makes driver timekeeping software. I have a bachelor’s degree and can sort most ordinary code faults, though the hard pay-rule cases need a specialist. I start with a disputed shift record, compare the clock-in times with the driver’s sheet, and test the correction. I use AI now and then to summarise long logs after a colleague showed me, but I still calculate the hours myself.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What depends on that work at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner, Mira, drives a bus, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. My pay is typical for a developer, and we have about three months of expenses saved. There are some similar jobs nearby. Mira’s hours can change with the route timetable, so we keep the household budget on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell our team AI Plateau means we still have to check time sheets and correct pay. A quick log summary is fine, but a driver needs the right hours on the payslip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I would be glad my own work stays steady. I would still watch the bus timetable, because three months of savings is not much if Mira loses a route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep matching driver sheets to clock-in records and use AI only to summarise long logs. I’d move 150 into savings after payday when Mira’s route hours hold. In the first year I’d ask payroll to keep the driver’s original sheet with each correction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the household, though I expect my own hours to hold. A timetable change can make our mortgage budget tight without any AI story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which time sheet error stays with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A driver once lost half a day’s pay when a break was counted twice. I laid both time sheets on the desk and found the repeated line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mira about the budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show Mira the paper budget each month rather than promise every route will stay. We can keep the children’s school activities while her hours are stable.

say: I expect **AI Plateau** to leave people checking time sheets and pay.
I would keep **original driver sheets** with corrected records.
think: I expect my **developer work** to stay steady.
I worry Mira’s **route hours** could change even without AI.
do: **Keep** matching driver sheets to clock-in records and checking AI log summaries.
**Save** 150 after payday when bus-route hours hold.
**Keep** original driver sheets with each correction.
feel: **Uneasy** about route hours, with my own work likely stable.
S0.quote: A timetable change can make our mortgage budget tight without any AI story.
fieldNote: He checks **AI summaries** against original driver records rather than adopting new tools blindly.
The **three-month reserve** is useful, but variable bus hours keep the mortgage on his mind.

steps.text: Keep checking driver sheets against clock records and AI log summaries
Save 150 after payday when bus-route hours hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption can draft timekeeping code and answer payroll questions faster. I would ask for an error trial before anyone lowers the number of people checking wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the company could move routine shift fixes to software and cut my hours. Mira still drives a bus, but her route office may also use AI for planning and bookings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d test the approved assistant on fourteen old double-break cases with the payroll clerk. If it catches them all, I’d learn to review its suggestions on copied records during paid work time. In the first year, if my hours fall, we’d suspend the planned weekend trip and keep the money for the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can see a useful tool, but my hours could shrink while bus schedules still set our other wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should sign the corrected hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the payroll clerk to sign the corrected hours before any new target is used. A speed chart cannot tell a driver how to pay a bill after missing a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you change the trip plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Mira about an actual hours cut, not a rumour. We would make the trip decision together after checking the next bus rota.

say: I expect **Steady Disruption** to speed code and payroll answers.
I would require an **error trial** before reducing wage checks.
think: I fear **routine shift fixes** could move to AI and shrink my hours.
I worry Mira’s **route office** may automate planning before driving changes.
do: **Test** the approved assistant on fourteen old double-break cases this month.
**Learn** its review screen on copied records during paid time only if all cases pass.
**Suspend** the weekend trip if my hours actually fall.
feel: **Anxious** about my wages and bus-route uncertainty.
S1.quote: A speed chart cannot tell a driver how to pay a bill after missing a shift.
fieldNote: His **fourteen-case trial** protects pay accuracy and gates any paid-time AI learning.
He cuts the **weekend trip** only after an actual hours loss and checking the next bus rota.

steps.text: Learn approved timekeeping AI during paid time if fourteen old cases pass
Suspend planned weekend trip only if developer hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2028 can do our timekeeping-code thinking work in 2028. Robots for hands-on driving arrive around 2031, so Mira’s bus job has more time than my desk job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect my developer role could end, and Mira’s driving may face robots later. Three months saved will not cover our mortgage through a long search and a second job shock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask my employer for written severance terms and keep the money planned for a new car in cash. Mira and I would check the mortgage, food and bus-commute bills first. In the first year after 2028, if dismissed, I’d apply for actual local openings and income help we qualify for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, because my salary could stop before Mira knows what happens to her routes. Three months of savings buys decisions, not a replacement pay packet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the car?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the current car if a mechanic says it is safe. We would pay for safety repairs but cancel the upgrade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our children the car can wait and their school travel stays. I would not promise that my next software job is nearby.

say: I expect **AGI by 2028** to reach timekeeping code before driving robots arrive.
I would tell colleagues Mira’s **bus work** has roughly three more years.
think: I expect my **developer role** could end.
Our **three-month savings** cannot cover mortgage and two possible job shocks.
do: **Cancel** the planned car upgrade and reserve cash for the mortgage.
**Request** written severance terms and review essential bills with Mira.
**Apply** for actual local openings and eligible income help if dismissed after 2028.
feel: **Alarmed** by likely lost pay before the driving change.
S2.quote: Three months of savings buys decisions, not a replacement pay packet.
fieldNote: His **code risk** arrives in 2028, with driving robots around 2031; bus-office thinking tasks may change earlier.
The **car upgrade** is cancelled while safety repairs remain funded; jobs and public help are conditional.

steps.text: Cancel planned car upgrade but fund safety repairs
Apply for real local jobs if dismissed after 2028
Apply for eligible income help if dismissed after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives five years to sort out how driver pay is checked. Thinking AI reaches my code in 2031; hands-on bus robots follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still think my coding role may shrink, but five years lets me learn more pay rules while wages continue. I do not assume payroll checking survives full thinking AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d take the company’s free pay-rules course if it is still offered and write up one disputed shift each month. I’d ask the payroll clerk to check my reasoning during normal work hours. In the first year after 2031, if my code work ends, I’d apply for real payroll-support openings that pay enough for the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the coding job, though I have time to prove I can understand complicated shifts. Mira and I could build the buffer if her routes stay steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you show payroll knowledge?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use the double-break case as my first written example and show how the corrected wage is calculated. A title on a course certificate would not prove I can do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the free course disappears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the company stops offering the free course, I’d use the public rules guide instead. I would not buy a costly certificate from the three-month reserve.

say: I see **AGI by 2031** as time to document driver-pay checks.
I know **2034 bus robots** follow the earlier code change.
think: I expect **coding hours** may shrink despite warning.
I cannot assume **payroll support** remains paid work after full thinking AI.
do: **Complete** the free pay-rules course if offered, or use the public guide.
**Write** one disputed-shift case monthly with payroll-clerk feedback during work.
**Apply** for real mortgage-paying payroll-support roles if coding ends after 2031.
feel: **Anxious** about code work, with time to learn if wages continue.
S3.quote: I do not assume payroll checking survives full thinking AI.
fieldNote: He tests a **specific pay skill** while earning, with free rules material if the course closes.
His **role search** requires real openings and mortgage-covering pay; he protects the three-month reserve.

steps.text: Study free pay rules and write monthly disputed-shift example with payroll feedback during work
Apply for actual payroll-support jobs paying mortgage if coding ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2036 leaves a decade to make driver pay records clearer. Thinking AI reaches code in 2036, while hands-on bus robots arrive around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect my pay to hold for now, though Mira’s timetable can still change. Three months saved is not so much that we can stop watching the budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking driver sheets against code and ask the payroll clerk to review one unusual case each month. I’d keep saving 150 after payday when Mira’s routes hold. In the first year after 2036, if code work ends, I’d search actual openings and compare pay before moving the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the long term, but my job and the mortgage look steady for the next few years. I can make a slower decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy the car in the longer runway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the current car until its repair cost exceeds what a safer replacement would cost us. I would not finance a new model just because the technology date is far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move the children for another job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mira and I would keep the children at their current school unless an actual job offer covers moving and a new mortgage. We would discuss the numbers before asking them to change schools.

say: I see **AGI by 2036** as time to improve driver-pay records.
I know **2039 bus robots** follow the code change.
think: I expect my **developer pay** to hold for now.
I still watch **route hours** and a limited three-month reserve.
do: **Keep** checking driver sheets with monthly payroll review.
**Save** 150 after payday only while Mira’s routes hold.
**Search** actual job openings after 2036 if coding work ends.
feel: **Uneasy** about long-term change, with near-term work stable.
S4.quote: Three months saved is not so much that we can stop watching the budget.
fieldNote: The **long horizon** supports careful decisions, but variable bus routes still shape savings.
A **family move** requires a real offer covering housing, and car replacement requires a cost comparison.

steps.text: Keep checking driver sheets with monthly payroll-clerk review
Save 150 after payday when bus routes hold
Search real openings if code work ends after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my code income could go before Mira’s driving work changes. Written severance, paid time to learn pay rules and eligible income help would help. Three months is a useful pause, not a new wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who tells a bus driver that a missing break erased half a day’s pay. A clean time sheet can still hide a lost wage.

headlineQuote: A clean time sheet can still hide a lost wage.
portrait: Erik is a **43-year-old mid-level developer** with a bachelor’s degree and average skill in driver timekeeping software.
He uses **AI occasionally** for logs, checking summaries against original shift and pay records.
His partner’s **bus driving** faces hands-on robots later, while route-office thinking tasks can change sooner.
Three months saved supports **careful trials**, free pay-rule study and job searches tied to real mortgage-paying openings.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his code pay before bus robots reach his partner’s work.
whatWouldHelp: **Written severance**, paid learning time and eligible income help would help.
